name: Persian Kabob Koobideh Rice Bowls
intro_html: Koobideh is the Persian kabob house classic: ground beef whipped with grated onion until it clings, then grilled into juicy, savory kabobs served over buttered rice. Ours skips the skewers, keeps the flavor, and stacks {{protein}} grams of protein into every bowl for about ${{cost_ps}} (at everyday cost).
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Rice, 4 cups dry: ~$1.04. Buy 1 (covers this batch with some left over).
Pantry seasonings (paprika, salt, black pepper, ground turmeric): ~$0.59. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $48.00 across 14 servings, so roughly $3.43 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $50.23 across 14 servings, roughly $3.59 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $6.94 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $57.17. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost) for a koobideh plate that kabob restaurants charge $16 to $18 for. This bowl is nearly all beef, which is why it costs more than our rice-heavy dishes and still embarrasses the restaurant price.
shop_smart:
This recipe is 7 pounds of beef, full stop. It is over 90 percent of the receipt, so shop it the week ground beef goes on sale and save real money.
Everything else in the bowl costs very little combined. Onion, garlic, butter, rice, spices. That is the whole supporting cast.
There is no marinade, no breadcrumbs, no filler to buy. The onion juice is the tenderizer, and it costs almost nothing.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Cook the rice: 3.75 cups dry with water per your usual method. Melt the butter into the hot rice and fluff.
Grate the onions on a box grater and squeeze the pulp firmly to remove most of the juice. Wet meat falls apart, so squeeze like you mean it.
Knead the beef with the squeezed onion, garlic, paprika, turmeric, salt, and pepper for a good 3 to 4 minutes until it turns sticky and pasty. That texture is what holds koobideh together.
Shape into long flat logs, about one wide log per serving, and press a light zigzag pattern in with your fingers, kabob-house style.
Broil on high on a foil-lined pan 4 to 5 minutes per side, or grill over hot coals, until browned outside with no pink in the middle.
Rest 5 minutes, then serve over the buttered rice with any pan juices poured back on top.
portion_html: Weigh your finished kabobs in the pot, subtract the empty pot number from step 1, and divide by 14, then do the same with the buttered rice. Each bowl lands at {{cal}} calories and a heavyweight {{protein}} grams of protein.

steps: Cook the rice and melt the butter into it.
Grate the onions and squeeze out the juice.
Knead beef with onion, garlic, and spices until sticky, then shape into flat logs.
Broil 4 to 5 minutes per side until browned with no pink inside.
Rest, then serve over buttered rice in 14 containers.
